chunks: "Low-side sensing puts the sense resistor between the load and ground. High-side puts it between the supply and the load.
Low-side is simple and cheap: the sense voltage sits near ground, so almost any amplifier or even an ADC can read it, and the common-mode problem disappears.

The downsides are that the load's ground is lifted by I R s , which can disturb other circuits, and it can't see a fault where the load or its wiring shorts to ground, because that current never goes through the shunt.
High-side keeps the load solidly grounded and does see a short to ground, because all the supply current goes through the shunt.
The cost is that the sense voltage rides on the bus voltage, so I need a current sense amplifier with high common-mode range and good CMRR.
That's more expensive and, for high voltages, needs level shifting or isolation.
So I use high-side when the load must be grounded, when I need short-to-ground detection, like battery or hot-swap protection, and for common-ground systems with multiple loads.
I use low-side when the system tolerates a small ground shift, the bus voltage is high or noisy, and I want the cheapest, simplest sense, like motor-driver legs or small embedded boards."
